course_name_original: MECCANICA RAZIONALE E SCIENZA DELLE COSTRUZIONI
course_name_en: RATIONAL MECHANICS AND STRENGTH OF MATERIALS
prerequisites: Basic mathematical knowledge, with particular reference to concepts and solution techniques inherent to integration theory and the resolution of ordinary differential equations.
In-depth knowledge of vector algebra and matrix theory.
Basic knowledge of physics (velocity, acceleration, force, etc.).

learning_outcomes.text: The student must know the basic elements of vector calculus for the study of kinematics and dynamics of a point, systems of points, and rigid bodies, also in the Lagrangian formalism. They must also be able to understand simple problems of mass geometry.

The student must be able to solve problems of mass geometry and dynamics of planar mechanical systems (constrained and unconstrained) by an appropriate choice of coordinates in the configuration space for writing the equations of motion.

The student must be able to autonomously deepen what has been learned, in order to use the acquired knowledge as a starting point that allows them to reach further results, characterized by increasing maturity and a broader autonomy of judgment.

The student must have the ability to explain in a simple, but detailed and precise manner, the methods and techniques adopted to solve a mechanics problem and the procedures used to arrive at the results obtained. They must also be able to explain, even to non-experts, to which practical experiences everything learned can be applied.

The student must be able to apply the acquired knowledge to contexts different from those presented during the course, as well as deepen the topics covered using alternative approaches and/or procedures. The student must also be able to continuously update themselves by consulting texts and/or publications.

The course aims to provide students of the Mechanical Engineering degree program with the theoretical and applied fundamentals of solid and structural mechanics, through the introduction of the basic concepts of continuous body, local stresses and deformations, constitutive laws and material strength criteria, as well as the in-depth study of statics and kinematics of planar framed structures, the technical beam theory, and resistance and stability checks.

The topics addressed aim to ensure the acquisition of a methodological approach for the design and structural verification of beam systems and for the analysis of the stress-strain state in continuous bodies.

The acquired knowledge allows the development of a critical and decision-making capacity of students for the correct modeling of beam systems subjected to external actions, the analysis of their mechanical behavior, and the experimentation of appropriate sizing and verification procedures.
The oral presentation of the topics covered contributes to the refinement of linguistic and communication properties.

The acquired approach method lends itself to being extended to more complex structural modeling and in different contexts from those presented during the course, through autonomous in-depth studies with the aid of specialized texts.

syllabus_topics: Vector calculus: free vectors and geometric-differential applications to curves.
Applied vectors: applied vectors. Central axis. Equivalence between systems of vectors.
Kinematics of a point: velocity. Acceleration. Planar motions. Central motions. Harmonic motion.

Kinematics of material systems: degrees of freedom. Kinematics of rigid systems. Particular rigid motions. Poisson's formulas. Mozzi's theorem. Instantaneous axis of roto-translation. Kinematics of relative motions. Planar rigid motions.

Statics and dynamics of a free material point: theorem of living forces for a free material system. Conservation of mechanical energy. Motion of a free point. Statics of a free material point. Harmonic oscillator, damped harmonic motion, resonance.
Statics and dynamics of a constrained material point: motion of a constrained point. Statics of a constrained point. Point constrained to a curve.
Geometry of masses: barycenter and properties. Momentum and angular momentum. Koenig's theorem. Kinetic energy and moments of inertia. Huygens' theorem.

General theorems of mechanics of material systems: cardinal equations of dynamics. Motion of the barycenter. Theorem of living forces and conservation of mechanical energy for a constrained material system.
Statics of a rigid body: cardinal equations of statics. Constraint reactions on a rigid body in equilibrium.
Dynamics of a rigid body: rigid body with a fixed axis without friction and constraint stresses.

Elements of analytical mechanics: virtual displacements for a holonomic system. Virtual work. Symbolic equation of dynamics and D'Alembert's principle. Symbolic equation of statics and principle of virtual works. Equilibrium conditions for a holonomic system. Holonomic systems subjected to conservative forces. Lagrange's equations.

Mechanics of continuous bodies: continuous body model, displacements and deformations, hypothesis of infinitesimal deformations, pure deformation and infinitesimal rigid rotation, external forces, stresses, principal directions of stress and deformation, indefinite equilibrium equations, boundary conditions, constitutive laws.
Geometry of areas: introduction, notations, change of reference, static moments, barycenter, moments of inertia.

Elastic problem of a straight beam: technical beam theory, generalized stresses and deformations, congruence equations, indefinite equilibrium equations, boundary conditions, linear elastic constitutive law, distortions, thermal distortions.

Planar beam systems: center of rotation, constraints and constraint reactions, kinematic problem, static problem and static-kinematic duality, theorems of kinematic chains, isostatic, hyperstatic and labile systems, constraint reactions, diagrams of internal stress characteristics, elastic line, force method.
Safety verifications: centered normal stress, straight bending, skewed bending, combined bending, shear and torsion, stress state in beams, resistance criteria, Eulerian critical load.
assessment_rules: For each module, there is a written exam and an oral exam. The written exams are typically held on the same day and consist of solving typical exercises presented in the course. The written exam for Rational Mechanics is graded from 0 to 30 (sum of scores from two exercises) and must be at least 18 to pass. The written exam for Strength of Materials consists of two exercises. Written exams are not cumulative. The oral exam for each module, contingent on passing the written exam, covers definitions, statements, and demonstrations of key topics, and verifies methodological rigor, language proficiency, and synthesis ability. For Rational Mechanics, the oral exam consists of three theoretical questions, each scored 0-10, with a minimum total of 18 to pass. For Strength of Materials, the oral exam consists of 6 theoretical and/or application questions, with a minimum score of 18 required for each response. The final grade for a single module is determined from the written exam score/band and considering the oral exam score. The final grade for the entire course is a weighted average of the final grades from the two modules, based on their respective ECTS credits. Honors ('Lode') require demonstration of high methodological and expository rigor, excellent language proficiency, and honors in at least one of the two oral exams.
